passage:
On his second Monday at the new school in Bengaluru, Asif opened his tiffin and the smell of sheermal and korma drifted across the room. Two boys wrinkled their noses. "What is that? Sooo spicy," one said, and the other copied the way Asif said "aap" until the bench laughed.
Asif closed the lid halfway and answered every question in one word. That evening he told his mother he wanted plain bread from tomorrow.
Karthik, at the next bench, had heard it all. "Can I try a piece?" he asked the next day, and afterwards handed over an idli. "Tell me how to say sheermal properly. I'll teach you some Kannada."
Asif packed the korma again.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling in his first weeks, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt homesick and self-conscious: he closed the lid halfway, gave one-word answers and asked his mother for plain bread.

qa.q: What could Asif do to settle in without losing himself?
qa.a: He can keep bringing food from home and speaking his own way, learn some Kannada slowly with Karthik, and keep the one or two allies close.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Asif's food?
qa.a: Karthik sees it as something to be curious about: he asks to try it and offers an idli in exchange, rather than wrinkling his nose.

grounding: A boy who moved to a new city is teased for his language and food, keeps his roots and finds an ally who trades words and food.

passage: Vikas's family had moved from Gaya to Bengaluru in the middle of term, and exams started in his second week. He didn't know a word of Kannada, and the boys at the back mimicked his Hindi, 'Kya re, sattu boy?', after they saw his tiffin. On the day of the Kannada oral, the power went out, the fans stopped, and he stood sweating at the board, forgetting even the greeting he'd practised. Laughter. He sat down, cheeks burning, thinking of his old school, where everyone knew his name. At lunch Yash, who had moved from Pune two years earlier, slid along the bench. 'I was the "Marathi boy" for a whole year. I'll teach you ten useful Kannada words, and you teach me what sattu actually is.' Vikas laughed. That evening Maa packed extra sattu: one tiffin for him, one for Yash.

qa.q: What happened during Vikas's Kannada oral?
qa.a: The power went out, the fans stopped, and he forgot even the greeting he'd practised.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he sat down after the oral?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and homesick, cheeks burning, missing his old school where everyone knew his name.

qa.q: What small step helped Vikas start to belong?
qa.a: Accepting Yash's offer to swap Kannada words for sattu, which keeps his roots while he learns local ways.

qa.q: How does Yash see Vikas's struggle?
qa.a: He recognises it from his own year as the 'Marathi boy', so he offers friendship and help.

grounding: Shows a teen who moved cities and is teased for his language and food, keeping his roots while finding an ally and learning local words.

passage: In her first month at school in Chennai, Zeenat learned that her pink noon chai drew stares. 'Strawberry milk tea?' someone sniggered at break, and another girl copied the way she said 'ji' after everything. Zeenat started leaving the flask at home and answering in short English words only. On Saturday, walking past the Mylapore temple tank with Papa, she heard an old man teaching a child Tamil numbers, and found herself repeating them under her breath. On Monday she brought the flask back. When Lokesh from her bench asked what it was, she poured him a little. 'Salty? Pink? Weird,' he said, then took another sip. 'Actually good.' He taught her 'romba nalla', very good, and she taught him the Kashmiri word for tea. By Friday two more people wanted to try it, and Zeenat said 'ji' as often as she liked.

qa.q: What did Lokesh teach Zeenat to say?
Why did Zeenat start leaving the flask at home?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and out of place after the sniggers, so she tried to hide what marked her as different.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Zeenat, and why?
qa.a: Bringing the flask back while also learning Tamil words, because she kept her roots and let an ally in 😊

qa.q: How does Lokesh see the noon chai?
qa.a: He finds it weird at first but is curious enough to taste it and decides it's actually good.

grounding: Shows a teen who moved to a new city and was teased for her language and food, keeping her roots, learning local ways and finding an ally.
